Using probability maps to guide kinetic Ising simulations

Jakub Nowosad

Source: vignettes/external-field.Rmd
external-field.Rmd

spatialising simulates changes in binary spatial patterns using two main pressures: the external pressure B and the local interaction strength J. Positive values of B favor class 1, negative values favor class -1, and larger absolute values have a stronger effect across the pattern. Larger values of J make neighboring cells more likely to have the same class, creating larger patches and reducing isolated cells.

By default, B is constant across all cells, but external_field allows a different adjustment for each cell, for example based on a spatial probability map. At cell ii, the effective external pressure is then B+𝚎𝚡𝚝𝚎𝚛𝚗𝚊𝚕_𝚏𝚒𝚎𝚕𝚍iB + \mathtt{external\_field}_i. Let’s see that on an example.

Probability map

We use the 2013 Maine forest pattern as the initial state and the 2016 pattern as a visual reference. The 2016 pattern is not used to create the probability map or choose the simulation parameters.

library(terra)
library(spatialising)

maine2013 = rast(system.file("raster/maine2013.tif", package = "spatialising"))
maine2016 = rast(system.file("raster/maine2016.tif", package = "spatialising"))

Moreover, we have a probability map p that represents the probability of each cell being class 1.

p = rast(system.file("raster/maine_probability.tif", package = "spatialising"))

In this example, the probability map is based only on the 2013 pattern and assumes that most cells keep their original class.1 We assume that cells at class boundaries are more likely to change than cells inside larger patches – so the boundary cells were given a 25% chance of changing class, compared with 5% for other cells. Because p is the probability of class 1, its possible values are 0.05, 0.25, 0.75, and 0.95.

names(maine2013) = "2013"
names(p) = "Probability of class 1"
names(maine2016) = "2016"
plot(c(maine2013, p, maine2016), nr = 1)

Simulation

The external_field argument of kinetic_ising() allows to use a spatially varying external pressure. Its values are in the same units as B, so we need to convert the probabilities in p to the pressure scale. The map p gives the probability that each cell belongs to class 1. To convert these probabilities to the model’s pressure scale, we take their log-odds and divide by two. Because B = 0 in this example, the converted values can be used directly as external_field:

B = 0
external_field = 0.5 * log(p / (1 - p)) - B

The value J = 0.3 (local interaction strength) is chosen only for this illustration. Using the same random seed makes it easier to compare the effect of the spatial field.

set.seed(1)
without_field = kinetic_ising(maine2013, B = B, J = 0.3)

set.seed(1)
with_field = kinetic_ising(maine2013, B = B, J = 0.3, external_field = external_field)

Compared with using B = 0 alone, the field makes core cells less likely to change while allowing more change at class boundaries.

names(without_field) = "Without external field"
names(with_field) = "With external field"
plot(c(without_field, with_field), nr = 1)

  1. But in practice, the probability map could be based on other spatial variables, such as elevation, distance to roads, or other environmental factors; or it could be a prediction from a machine learning model.↩︎
